headline: Oliver Hitchcock and co-authors trace the microsecond ceiling on piezoelectric acoustic resonators to ion-mill damage rather than to lithium niobate itself, and reach a 21-millisecond phonon lifetime at 3.6 GHz once the damaged surface is etched off.

items.title: Piezoelectric acoustic loss was ion-mill damage, not the material
items.dek: Oliver Hitchcock, Amir Safavi-Naeini and co-authors built phononic-crystal resonators — patterned slabs that trap a 3.6 GHz sound wave in a defect at their centre — from lithium niobate and measured phonon lifetimes up to 21 milliseconds, four orders of magnitude past previous piezoelectric devices, after chemically stripping the damage their ion mill had left.
items.why_it_matters: Piezoelectric films were believed to carry an intrinsic acoustic loss that electrostatic silicon resonators do not, which forced designers to choose between strong electrical coupling and long mechanical coherence; the ceiling turns out to sit in the process, so the trade is not a property of the solid. The product of coupling and quality factor — the figure that decides how hard a microwave circuit can drive a mechanical mode before the mode decays — moves from below about 10⁴ to between 1.3 × 10⁵ and 8.6 × 10⁵, and what now limits the measurement is the wiring rather than the crystal.
items.background_md: A piezoelectric resonator turns a voltage into mechanical strain and back, which is how a radio filter or a mechanical quantum memory gets addressed electrically. Its quality factor counts how many cycles the stored sound survives, and in a thin film the loss is concentrated at the surfaces: the top few nanometres of any etched film are left disordered, and disordered solids contain two-level systems — atoms with two nearly degenerate configurations — that absorb strain energy. The fraction of the mode's energy sitting in those surface layers rises as the film is thinned, so the smallest devices pay the most.
items.deeper_md:
The devices are quasi-1D phononic crystals in 150 nm X-cut MgO-doped lithium niobate over 3 µm of buried oxide, with a central defect cell roughly 550–700 nm × 950–1100 nm hosting a shear mode between 3.35 and 4.20 GHz. The process is the result. An SC1 wet etch thins the film to remove ion-mill damage; after release in hydrofluoric acid the chip is cleaned in SC1 again to strip the amorphous layer; only then is 50 nm of aluminium evaporated through a bonded silicon-nitride stencil, because resist liftoff would leave organics on a surface that can no longer be cleaned aggressively.

Sweeping the electrode gap separates external from internal loss: at 360 nm the measured T₁ is 5.0 µs, at 4760 nm it is 4.9 ms, and the inferred internal value is 21 ± 6 ms with external coupling κ_e/2π falling from about 12 kHz to 25 Hz.

The authors' own caveats: the 21 ms is an inference carrying ±6 ms, the two-level-system attribution rests on their earlier loss-channel work rather than on a measurement here, and stencil yield is 10–20 % at the narrowest gap. Congruent lithium niobate holds roughly one niobium antisite per cubic nanometre, so bulk defects are the plausible next floor.

glossary.definition: How long a quantum of sound survives in a resonator before its energy leaks away; it equals Q/(2πf), so 21 ms at 3.6 GHz corresponds to a quality factor near 5 × 10⁸.
Frequency multiplied by quality factor; several loss mechanisms scale so that this product rather than Q alone characterises a material, and above 10¹⁸ is the best reported for a piezoelectric film.
A defect in a disordered solid with two nearly equal-energy configurations; it couples to strain and drains energy from a mechanical mode, dominating loss at millikelvin temperatures.

The fraction of a resonator's stored energy that is electrical rather than mechanical; it sets how strongly a circuit can drive the mode, and is what piezoelectrics buy at the usual price of extra loss.

items.fab_angle: The order of operations is the whole trick: once a surface has been cleaned to this standard it can never see photoresist again, so metal goes down last through a stencil bonded in a flip-chip aligner. Any lab that ion-mills a film and then patterns metal by liftoff is building in the damage layer this work removes.

sources.title: Millisecond phonon lifetimes in piezoelectric nanomechanical resonators

items.title: Monolayer channels have band edges ten times blurrier than silicon
items.dek: Zherui Han, Eric Pop and co-authors argue that the exponential tail of electronic states smeared into a monolayer semiconductor's band gap — about 100 meV wide, against roughly 10 meV in silicon — is what caps the mobility and the turn-on sharpness of two-dimensional transistors, and has to fall below about 50 meV before the devices are worth building.
items.why_it_matters: Band tails are not a defect population you can anneal away one site at a time, because they come from long-range potential fluctuation imposed by whatever sits above and below a channel two atoms thick; the available fixes are therefore electrostatic and mechanical — more gate capacitance, strain, a bilayer instead of a monolayer. That turns a vague materials-quality argument into one measurable number, the Urbach energy, which can be read off an absorption or emission edge on a film long before anyone fabricates a transistor on it.
items.background_md: A transistor switches sharply only if its band edge is sharp. Were the density of states to fall abruptly to zero at the conduction-band edge, drain current would drop tenfold for every 60 mV of gate swing at room temperature — the thermal limit. Real disordered material instead leaks states exponentially into the gap, with a characteristic width called the Urbach energy, and carriers occupying those states are localised rather than mobile. The thinner the channel, the worse this gets, because there is no bulk to screen the charges trapped in the dielectric below or adsorbed on the surface above.
items.deeper_md:
The claim is built from a physics-based electrical model compared against published device data rather than from new silicon, and the paper is explicit that the three proposed remedies — raising gate capacitance, strain engineering, and a bilayer channel — only pay off if the Urbach energy drops under roughly 50 meV. The supporting evidence that the slow-turn-on problem is real and not an artefact of poor gate coupling arrived the same week: a Nature Communications group using a carbon-dot van der Waals interfacial layer to put HfO₂ directly on MoS₂ reports an equivalent oxide thickness of 0.8–0.9 nm — close to the best anyone has achieved on a 2D channel — and still measures an average subthreshold swing of 120 ± 20 mV/dec across 28 devices, with the minimum only approaching 60.

The caveat is in the tail's origin. Earlier Green's-function work on transition-metal dichalcogenides finds band tails depending on layer count, temperature, doping and, strongly, on the substrate, which means the 100 meV figure is a property of a stack rather than of a material and can be argued down by changing what the sheet sits on.

glossary.definition: The width of the exponential tail of states that disorder smears into a semiconductor's band gap, read off the slope of an absorption or emission edge plotted on a log scale.
The gate voltage needed to change drain current tenfold; room-temperature statistics put a floor near 60 mV per decade, and band tails push a real device above it.
Carrier drift velocity per unit field, averaged over every carrier the gate has induced; it falls when some of those carriers sit immobile in localised tail states.
The thickness of plain SiO₂ that would give the same gate capacitance as the real dielectric stack; a smaller number means tighter gate control over the channel.

items.fab_angle: This argues for measuring an absorption or photoluminescence edge on a new 2D film before anyone builds a transistor on it, because the tail width predicts the swing and takes an optical bench rather than a probe station.

sources.title: Band Tail States: Speed Bump or End of the Road for Two-Dimensional Semiconductors?

items.title: Forming-free switching from a p–n oxide stack, at a window of only ten
items.dek: Dip Manna and co-authors sputtered titanium oxide onto crystalline nickel oxide and got a memristor — a two-terminal device whose resistance remembers the last voltage applied to it — that switches without the one-time high-voltage electroforming step such cells normally need, because the junction between the two oxides breaks down softly under reverse bias instead.
items.why_it_matters: Electroforming is the step that makes resistive memory awkward to put on a chip: it wants a voltage above what the surrounding CMOS can comfortably deliver, it has to be applied cell by cell, and because dielectric breakdown is stochastic it is a leading source of device-to-device spread. A stack that forms itself trades that away for a resistance ratio of only about ten between the two states, which is the honest position of this class of device — the integration problem gets easier and the sense-amplifier problem gets harder.
items.background_md: Resistive memory stores a bit as the presence or absence of a conducting filament through a thin insulating oxide. The filament is built from oxygen vacancies — oxygen atoms missing from the lattice, leaving behind donor-like states that conduct — herded into a chain by the electric field and the Joule heat it generates. Creating the first filament takes a stronger field than switching it afterwards, because a pristine oxide has almost no vacancies to recruit; published simulation of a 10 nm hafnium-oxide cell puts that forming voltage between about 1.2 V and 2.5 V depending on which metal sits on top.
items.deeper_md:
The stack is Ag / TiOx ≈ 30 nm / NiOx ≈ 90 nm / p⁺⁺-Si, deposited by DC reactive magnetron sputtering in 5:1 Ar:O₂ at 5 mTorr, with the NiOx grown at room temperature. Set is at about +2.32 V and reset at about −2.50 V with a 100 mA compliance and no forming sweep. The growth result is the more transferable one: NiOx on silicon shows roughly 7 nm grains, TiOx grown on that NiOx shows roughly 21 nm grains, and TiOx deposited straight onto silicon shows no distinct grains at all — the underlying oxide is supplying nucleation sites.

The weaknesses are stated. The window is about 10×, retention is shown to 1.1 × 10⁴ s at a 2.0 V read, endurance is 300 cycles, and the 95 % MNIST figure comes from a network simulated with measured conductances against a 98 % ideal baseline, not from an array. The mechanism is contestable: post-switching TEM shows silver migrating into the TiOx, which points at an electrochemical-metallisation filament rather than the oxygen-vacancy one the authors invoke — a different device class with different failure modes.

glossary.definition: The one-time voltage sweep that creates the first conducting filament in a fresh resistive-memory cell; it needs a higher field than later switching because the pristine oxide has few vacancies to recruit.
A missing oxygen atom in an oxide lattice; it leaves donor-like electronic states behind, and a connected chain of them is what carries current in a filamentary memory.
High- and low-resistance state, the two values a memristor is read as; their ratio is the memory window, and a ratio near ten leaves a sense amplifier very little margin.
Resistive switching in which set and reset require opposite voltage polarities, as against unipolar switching, where both happen at one polarity and are separated by current level.

items.fab_angle: Every deposition here is room-temperature reactive sputtering onto a degenerate silicon wafer after an RCA clean and a 1 % HF dip, and the central claim — that the grain size of the top oxide is set by the oxide beneath it — is checkable with an AFM. That is within reach of a teaching cleanroom with a sputterer.

sources.title: Multifunctional synaptic learning and neuromorphic computing using crystalline TiOx/NiOx heterojunction-based memory devices

items.title: A second fab for the interposer that carries the decoupling capacitors
items.dek: GlobalFoundries said on 8 October it will make silicon interposers — the passive slab of silicon that fans the wiring out between an AI accelerator and its memory stacks — for TSMC's CoWoS packaging at its Malta, New York fab, including versions with deep trench capacitors etched into the interposer itself, ramping in the first half of 2028.
items.why_it_matters: Capacitors in the interposer are how a 2.5D package holds its supply rail up when a few hundred amps of accelerator current switch on inside a nanosecond, and the reason they have to be in the interposer is distance: TSMC's own disclosure of the technique reports up to 340 nF/mm² and about 68 µF per interposer die, which is capacitance no board-mounted part centimetres away can deliver in time. Siting that process in a second fab says the constraint being relieved is interposer wafer starts in a mature-node line, not accelerator wafer starts at the leading edge.
items.background_md: A 2.5D package sets a logic die and several memory stacks side by side on a slab of silicon whose only job is wiring. Vias etched through the whole wafer thickness carry power and ground up from the package substrate, and a few micron-pitch copper layers carry the thousands of signals between the dies. The interposer exists because an organic substrate cannot hold wiring that fine and because the assembled die area exceeds a single exposure field. Its geometry is a generation or two behind logic — micron-class lines, not nanometre-class — so it is built in older fabs.
items.deeper_md:
Neither company named a process node, a capacitance, or a wafer volume, so the technical content has to come from elsewhere. GlobalFoundries' published interposer platform, 65PKG, is a 65 nm flow with three or four layers of 1.2 µm-thick copper at a 0.8 µm minimum critical dimension, 1.6 µm interlayer vias, and 10 µm × 100 µm through-silicon vias usable for signal, power and ground; the company describes it as production-qualified and already running at Malta.

The deep trench capacitor is the part with a number behind it. TSMC's IEDM 2019 paper on integrating high-κ deep trench capacitors into a CoWoS interposer reports up to 340 nF/mm² across a large array, roughly 68 µF per die, and a time-dependent dielectric breakdown lifetime above 1,000 years extrapolated at 1.35 V and 105 °C, with no measurable process-induced damage. That paper is paywalled and these figures come from its abstract.

Two caveats. Volume ramp is targeted for the first half of 2028, so nothing about interposer supply changes this year. And an agreement with a framework for later expansion is not a capacity number.

glossary.definition: A passive silicon slab beneath a package's dies; it carries their interconnect in micron-pitch copper layers and routes power up through vias drilled through the full wafer thickness.
A capacitor formed by etching narrow trenches tens of microns into silicon and lining them with dielectric, so a large plate area fits into a small footprint.
Capacitance per unit of silicon area; it decides whether on-package decoupling can replace board-level capacitors that are too far away to respond at nanosecond timescales.
A metal-filled hole etched through the whole thickness of a wafer; GlobalFoundries' published interposer platform uses vias 10 µm wide and 100 µm deep.

items.title: Python 3.15 binds an imported name without running the module
items.dek: Hugo van Kemenade released Python 3.15 on 9 October with a new lazy keyword that binds a module name to a placeholder object and defers finding and executing that module until the first time the name is read, a change PEP 810 reports cutting command-line tool startup time by 50 to 70 per cent.
items.why_it_matters: Deferring an import moves two other things with it. The module's side effects go too, so a class registration or a plugin hook that used to happen at import time may now never happen at all; and so do its errors, so a missing dependency or a module-level exception surfaces at the first attribute read rather than at startup, far from the line that caused it. That is why the feature is opt-in per statement instead of the default, and why it is the first supported replacement for the long-standing workaround of hiding an import inside a function — which PEP 810 counts in roughly 17 per cent of non-test standard-library imports.
items.background_md: An import statement in Python does work the moment it runs: it locates the module, executes its top-level code, and binds the resulting object to a name. Executing top-level code is both the expensive part and the part with consequences — it can register classes, open files, and import further modules in a chain hundreds deep. A program that imports a heavy library for one rarely-taken branch therefore pays the full cost on every run, including the runs that only print a usage message and exit.
items.deeper_md:
The mechanism is a proxy. `lazy import json` binds the name immediately to a `types.LazyImportType` object; the first read of that name calls the import machinery, which means it sees whatever import state exists at that moment rather than at the statement. The proxy is then replaced by the real object, so later reads are indistinguishable from an eager import. Lazy modules appear in `sys.lazy_modules` rather than `sys.modules`, and `globals()`, `__dict__` and `dir()` deliberately do not trigger resolution. A failed resolution leaves the proxy in place and retries on the next access, with the traceback chaining the import site to the access site. It is module-scope only: no function bodies, no `try` blocks, no star imports, no `__future__`.

The measured claims are uneven. The 50–70 % startup and 30–40 % memory figures are described as real-world observations, while the PEP's own benchmark table — 161.2 ms eager against 161.4–162.0 ms lazy — measures only the filter's overhead and sits inside its error bars. PEP 690, the earlier attempt to make laziness the default by changing the dict type, was rejected on core-performance grounds.

glossary.definition: An import whose name is bound at once to a proxy object, while the module itself is located and executed only when the name is first read.
The moment a lazy import's proxy is replaced by the real module or attribute; the import machinery runs then, so it observes the import state at access time rather than at the statement.
The subset of CPython's C interface a compiled extension may rely on across releases, so one binary wheel serves many versions; abi3t is the new variant that covers the free-threaded build.
CPython's standard benchmark suite; the 7–8 per cent geometric-mean figure quoted for the experimental JIT is measured against it, not against any single program.

items.title: Demote a cold page all the way down, not one tier at a time
items.dek: Mingyang Liu and co-authors measured that Linux's existing multi-tier memory managers fail more than 90 per cent of the page promotions they attempt, because the faster tier is already full, and cut that to between 31 and 40 per cent by sending cold pages straight to the slowest tier instead of stepping them down one tier at a time.
items.why_it_matters: A promotion only helps if there is room where the page is going, so in a four-tier machine the useful product of a demotion is not where the cold page lands but how much headroom it frees; stepping a page down one tier at a time spends migrations filling the middle tiers that the next promotion then has to clear again. The asymmetry also yields a cheap sampling rule — scan the slowest tier often to catch pages waking up, scan the fast tiers rarely to find cold ones — which is why the reported gain on a graph workload under memory pressure is 2.16× over Linux's own tiering mode rather than a few per cent.
items.background_md: A server's memory is no longer one pool. Local DRAM, a second socket's DRAM reached across the interconnect, and byte-addressable memory on a PCIe-class link differ by roughly a factor of four in latency and twenty in bandwidth, and the operating system presents each as a separate NUMA node whose rated latency and bandwidth it reads out of firmware tables and exports through sysfs. Software then has to decide which pages live where and move them as access patterns shift — and every move costs a page-table update plus an interrupt to every core that might hold a stale translation.
items.deeper_md:
The testbed is two Xeon Gold 6330 sockets, each with 96 GB of DDR4 and 256 GB of Optane persistent memory, on Linux 5.15. Measured tier latencies are 105 ns local DRAM, 171 ns remote DRAM, 327 ns local persistent memory and 420 ns remote, with bandwidths of 121, 55 and 5 GB/s and 600 MB/s. Against AutoNUMA, Tiering-0.8 and AutoTiering, the baselines average over 90 % promotion failures — 97.4 % on Silo and 99.4 % on Liblinear for AutoTiering — while the new scheme averages 39.5 % and 31.2 % in the two capacity ratios tested, for 70.2 % and 20.6 % over the second-best system. The profiling saving is concrete: scanning at one second per 1280 MB instead of per 256 MB, with unmap cost 246.7 ns against 271.0 ns and metadata overhead 0.2 %.

The caveat is the hardware. Compute Express Link is the stated motivation but the measurements are DRAM plus Optane, a discontinued product whose latencies are not a CXL device's, and there is no comparison against TPP, the proactive-demotion mechanism whose patches largely landed in Linux 5.18 and whose authors measured it within 1 % of an all-local baseline.

glossary.definition: A machine whose memory arrives in pools of different latency and bandwidth, presented to the operating system as separate NUMA nodes rather than as one uniform address space.
Migrating a page to a faster or a slower memory tier; a promotion fails outright when the destination tier has no free capacity, which is the failure these systems keep hitting.
The inter-processor interrupt that makes every core discard a cached virtual-to-physical translation after a page moves; it is the dominant cost in a migration.
The PCIe-based protocol that lets a host address memory on an attached device as ordinary byte-addressable memory, at roughly PCIe latency rather than DIMM latency.

sources.title: Mole: Tier-Specific Hotness Profiling Driven Memory Tiering for Multi-Tiered Memory Systems

items.title: An adversarial suffix makes speculative decoding slower than not using it
items.dek: Adam Jones, Yu Yuan and Sergio Maffeis showed that appending an optimised string to attacker-controlled text inside a prompt makes a large language model reject the tokens its small draft model proposes, pushing the mean accepted length per verification pass from 5.68 tokens down to 1.77 and the measured speed-up from 3.40× to 1.42×.
items.why_it_matters: Speculative decoding is a large part of why a serving stack can reach interactive latency, and its gain is not a constant: it is the average number of draft tokens the big model happens to agree with, which is a property of the text being generated and therefore of whatever an attacker managed to put into the prompt. That converts a throughput optimisation into an availability surface — in the worst measured configurations the attacked system runs at 0.90× to 0.96× of plain one-token-per-pass decoding, so the speculation is pure wasted compute.
items.background_md: Generating one token from a large language model costs one forward pass over all its weights, and that pass is limited by reading the weights out of memory rather than by arithmetic, so most of the arithmetic hardware sits idle. Speculative decoding spends the idle arithmetic: a small draft model proposes several tokens, the large model scores all of them in a single pass, and a sampling rule accepts the longest prefix the large model would itself have produced. The output distribution is unchanged, which is the appeal — and the speed-up is therefore exactly the average accepted prefix length.
items.deeper_md:
The target is Vicuna-13B v1.3 against seven drafting methods (SpS, Medusa, Hydra, EAGLE, EAGLE-2, EAGLE-3, PLD) on GSM8K, HumanEval and CNN/DailyMail. Task-average reductions under greedy decoding run from 10.1 % to 42.6 % in accepted length, with the worst single case EAGLE-3 on CNN/DailyMail: 5.68 tokens to 1.77, 3.40× to 1.42×, so roughly 3.2 times as many target-model passes per output token. Under sampling at temperature 1, EAGLE-3 on the same task reaches 0.96× against a clean 2.78×, and one SpS configuration reaches 0.90×. A random 20-token suffix moves accepted length by at most 0.04, so this is optimisation and not padding.

The exposure is uneven and partly defensible. Medusa and Hydra's typical-acceptance rule resists the attack — the reduction falls from 22.4 % to 18.2 % — and suffixes transfer badly across target models, retaining only 12–43 % of their effect from 13B to 7B. A fluency regulariser recovers 70–93 % of the lost output quality but gives back 66–95 % of the slowdown. No defence is evaluated experimentally; the authors note that a fluency term is exactly what defeats a perplexity filter.

glossary.definition: Running a small model to propose several next tokens and the large model to check them in one forward pass, accepting the longest prefix the large model would have generated itself.
The average number of draft tokens the target model accepts per verification pass; end-to-end speed-up is roughly proportional to it, so halving it halves the benefit.
A short string found by optimisation rather than written by hand, appended to text in order to steer a model — here to maximise disagreement between draft and target.
Generating one token per forward pass of the full model with no draft; it is the 1.0× baseline that speculative decoding must beat to be worth running.

sources.title: Speedbumps: Rejection Attacks on Speculative Decoding
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding

foundations.subtitle: Nothing useful transmits at 13.5 nm, so every optical surface in an EUV scanner is a fifty-layer interference stack — and the whole train still delivers under one per cent of the light.
foundations.tldr: At 13.5 nm there are no lenses, because every solid absorbs that light and so does air. What an EUV scanner uses instead is a stack of about fifty alternating molybdenum and silicon layers, each a couple of nanometres thick, spaced so the feeble reflections from every buried interface come back in step and add to roughly 70 per cent. Almost everything else about the machine — the vacuum, the mirror count, the kilowatts of drive laser feeding the source — follows from that 70 per cent and from the fact that it multiplies.

sections.heading: Why there is no lens
sections.body_md:
Start with the photon. Dividing 1239.8 eV·nm by 13.5 nm gives 91.8 eV, which is larger than the binding energy of every valence electron and of a good many core electrons too. Light at that energy does not politely slow down inside a material the way visible light does; it ionises atoms, which means absorption rather than refraction is the dominant interaction, and it means a few hundred nanometres of anything is opaque. Air is a material, so the whole optical path from source to wafer runs in vacuum.

The second half of the problem is less obvious. Because the electrons barely respond, the refractive index of every material at 13.5 nm sits within a whisker of vacuum's value of one — and the Fresnel reflection from a single interface scales with the index difference across it. So a perfectly polished surface at near-normal incidence sends back almost nothing. You cannot refract the light and you cannot mirror it either. What is left is interference.

sections.heading: A mirror built out of fifty weak reflections
sections.body_md:
If one interface returns a thousandth of the light, use a thousand interfaces and arrange for their returns to arrive in phase. That is the Bragg condition: stack alternating materials with period d so that the round trip through one period differs by a whole wavelength, 2d·cos θ = mλ. At near-normal incidence and first order this puts d close to λ/2, and the measured article agrees — a recent study of production-style coatings fitted periods of 6.97 to 7.07 nm with 50 bilayers.

The split inside the period is not even. The same fits give molybdenum 1.95 to 2.14 nm and silicon 3.70 to 3.84 nm, because molybdenum is the more absorbing of the pair: you give it the smaller share and let silicon carry most of the optical path while molybdenum supplies the scattering contrast. Note what this makes a mirror. Reflection here is not a surface property but a resonance of the whole stack, which is why it works only in a narrow band of wavelength and of incidence angle.
sections.deeper_md: The pairing is not arbitrary. Silicon is unusually weakly absorbing just on the long-wavelength side of its L-shell absorption edge, which falls a little below 13.5 nm, and molybdenum supplies contrast there without absorbing too much — so a usable window opens, and 13.5 nm sits inside it. The wavelength was chosen to fit the mirror rather than the reverse, and the fact that a laser-heated tin droplet emits brightly at the same wavelength is the other half of why the industry settled there. Absorption also decides how many bilayers are worth depositing: light reaching layer 60 has already crossed 59 molybdenum layers, so each further period contributes less than the one before and the stack saturates. The study below used 50.

sections.heading: Where the missing thirty per cent goes
sections.body_md:
A stack that reflects 70 per cent is throwing away three photons in ten, and most of that loss is at the interfaces rather than in the bulk. Grazing-incidence X-ray fits on real coatings show the two interfaces in a period are not alike: the molybdenum-grown-on-silicon boundary fits as 0.80 nm wide, while silicon-grown-on-molybdenum fits as 0.39 to 0.41 nm. The authors attribute the width mainly to interdiffusion rather than roughness — in other words, molybdenum silicide is forming. On a molybdenum layer only about 2 nm thick, 0.8 nm of silicide is a large fraction of a layer whose entire job is to be optically different from silicon.

This is why real coatings carry thin barrier layers between the silicon and the molybdenum, and why modelling a multilayer means modelling its interfaces. The standard treatment multiplies each interface's reflection coefficient by a Névot–Croce factor derived from an assumed error-function profile of given root-mean-square width, which is the knob you will turn yourself in the exercise below.
sections.deeper_md: The asymmetry is a growth effect rather than a measurement artefact: the two boundaries in a period are formed by different arriving species landing on different surfaces, and they intermix by different amounts under identical deposition conditions. That suggests a barrier is worth more on one of the two interfaces than on the other, which matters because every nanometre of barrier is a nanometre of period contributing neither contrast nor transparency. For scale on what is at stake: the curved-mirror study measured a peak near 65 per cent in the 12–15 nm range, against the roughly 70 per cent quoted for production coatings, and that five-point gap is what interface engineering is fighting over.

sections.heading: The photon budget, and why it multiplies
sections.body_md:
Here is the number that shapes the whole machine. At about 70 per cent per mirror, a six-mirror projection lens transmits 0.70⁶, which is roughly 12 per cent — and engineers at Cymer, who built the sources, put the whole optical train including the illuminator and the reflective mask at under 1 per cent. The collector that gathers light from the plasma peaks above 55 per cent on its own.

Everything upstream exists to pay that bill. In the pilot-generation sources those authors describe, an 11 kW carbon-dioxide laser hits tin droplets at better than 3 per cent conversion efficiency to produce over 300 W of EUV, of which more than 100 W reaches the intermediate focus where the scanner takes delivery.

The design rule that follows is blunt: every additional reflecting surface costs about 30 per cent of the light, so EUV optical designs are judged on mirror count before anything else. One recent proposal reaches numerical aperture 0.5 with four mirrors; it also abandons scanning for an 18 × 18 mm square stepper field, after radial distortion of a few microns at the rim of its 26 mm circular field proved to blur a scanned image.
sections.deeper_md: Two arithmetic checks worth doing by hand. First, 0.70⁶ = 0.118, which matches the quoted 12 per cent — so the six-mirror figure really is nothing but the per-mirror number raised to the sixth power, with no hidden losses. Second, extend it: 0.70¹¹ = 0.020, so eleven reflecting surfaces land near 2 per cent before the mask's own absorption and the illuminator's non-ideal pupil are counted, which is how you get to the sub-1 per cent figure. Those numbers are from 2009, before high-volume EUV manufacturing, and both source power and collector lifetime have improved considerably since — but the per-mirror reflectance has not moved much, because it is set by interface physics rather than by engineering effort.

sections.heading: The period has to change across the mirror
sections.body_md:
The Bragg condition contains cos θ, so a stack tuned for 13.5 nm at normal incidence is detuned wherever the light arrives at an angle. In a real projection system the beam converges, so the local incidence angle varies across a single curved mirror — over 5° to 17° on the collector described by the Cymer team, which they handle by grading the period about 5 per cent from centre to edge.

That is a brutal manufacturing requirement, and the curved-mirror study is a good window into it. Depositing by DC magnetron sputtering with the substrate in planetary rotation and a shadow mask fixed to the holder, the group held the intended period to within ±0.02 nm — about ±0.3 per cent — at every measured position across a 200 mm aperture, with surface roughness under 0.2 nm rms. Think about what ±0.02 nm means: a tolerance smaller than an atomic spacing, enforced across a curved surface the size of a dinner plate, and then repeated fifty times in a stack.
sections.deeper_md: A shadow mask works because planetary rotation turns a fixed aperture into a controlled residence-time profile: a point on the substrate that spends less time in the flux receives a thinner layer, so cutting an aperture of the right shape converts the deposition source's natural non-uniformity into the radial grading the optical design asks for. The trade is deposition rate — material intercepted by the mask is material that did not land on the mirror. Note also what the ±0.3 per cent period tolerance buys: because the reflectance peak is narrow, a 1 per cent period error shifts the peak wavelength by about 1 per cent, which is a substantial fraction of the stack's bandwidth and therefore shows up directly as lost intensity at 13.5 nm.

sections.heading: Keeping a mirror alive next to a tin plasma
sections.body_md:
The collector sits a short distance from a plasma that is made by vaporising tin, which means it is being plated and sandblasted continuously. The Cymer authors quantify the plating: roughly 1 nm of tin on the surface costs more than 10 per cent of the reflectivity. Their mitigation reduced ion energy by an order of magnitude and ion flux by four orders of magnitude, and the coating itself carries several hundred sacrificial layers on top of the optical stack, with a target of a year of operation before the collector is replaced or reconditioned.

The reason contamination hurts so specifically is the resonance. A stack's reflectance depends on fifty period thicknesses all staying where they were deposited, so any process that moves atoms — tin burial, oxidation, interdiffusion driven by the absorbed heat — detunes the mirror rather than merely dimming it. Thermal stability is therefore specified, not assumed: the coatings in that work showed no reflectivity loss over more than 100 hours at 500 °C after an initial anneal.
sections.deeper_md: The anneal is the detail worth noticing: the stability figure is quoted for the coating *after* annealing, not as deposited. That is the standard way to stabilise an interference stack — drive the interface reaction toward completion before the mirror goes into service, so it does not keep reacting under thermal load and detuning itself. The price is paid in reflectance, because the silicide formed deliberately during the anneal is the same silicide that cost contrast in the section above. That is the standing trade in EUV coating work, and which side of it a given mirror is optimised for depends on whether it sits beside the plasma or deep inside the projection optics.

glossary.definition: Light near 13.5 nm wavelength, about 92 eV per photon. Because it is absorbed by essentially every material including air, it is used only in vacuum and only with reflective optics.

The path-difference rule that makes reflections from a periodic stack add in phase, 2d·cos θ = mλ. For 13.5 nm at near-normal incidence and first order it puts the period close to 6.9 nm, which is why Mo/Si stacks are built at about 7 nm.

One repeat of the stack — here one molybdenum layer of roughly 2 nm plus one silicon layer of roughly 3.8 nm. The number of repeats decides how much of the weak per-interface reflection accumulates before absorption eats the remainder, which saturates near 50.

The correction applied to each interface's reflection coefficient to represent an interface of finite width rather than an abrupt step, assuming an error-function profile of a given rms thickness. It is how interdiffusion and roughness enter a multilayer calculation.
Surface roughness at short lateral scales, specified below 0.2 nm for EUV mirror substrates. Unlike long-scale figure error, it scatters light out of the image entirely rather than misplacing it.

The small aperture where the collected light from the plasma source is handed over to the scanner's illuminator. EUV source power is quoted there rather than at the plasma, because that is what the optics actually receive.

foundations.try_this: Build the mirror from section two yourself in the CXRO multilayer reflectivity calculator at henke.lbl.gov/optical_constants/multi2.html. Set the top material to Mo and the bottom to Si, period 7.0 nm, bottom-layer-to-period ratio 0.55, sigma 0, substrate Si, polarisation 1, and scan wavelength from 12 to 15 nm. Run it at 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 periods and note where the peak stops growing — that is absorption telling you how many bilayers are worth depositing. Then set sigma to 0.8 nm, the molybdenum-on-silicon interface width fitted in the Micromachines study, and read off what interdiffusion costs you. Finally raise 0.70 to the eleventh power by hand and compare it with the under-1-per-cent full-train transmission Cymer's engineers quote.
